{{Short description|Type of mathematical function}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''symmetric decreasing rearrangement''' of a function is a function which is symmetric and decreasing, and whose [[level sets]] are of the same size as those of the original function.<ref name=liebloss>{{cite book|last1=Lieb|first1=Elliott|authorlink1=Elliott H. Lieb|last2=Loss|first2=Michael|author2-link=Michael Loss|title=Analysis|year=2001|edition=2nd|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics|volume=14|isbn=978-0821827833}}</ref>

==Definition for sets==

Given a [[measurable set]], <math>A,</math> in <math>\R^n,</math> one defines the ''symmetric rearrangement'' of <math>A,</math> called <math>A^*,</math> as the ball centered at the origin, whose volume ([[Lebesgue measure]]) is the same as that of the set <math>A.</math> 

An equivalent definition is
<math display=block>A^* = \left\{x \in \R^n :\,\omega_n\cdot|x|^n < |A|\right\},</math>
where <math>\omega_n</math> is the volume of the [[unit ball]] and where <math>|A|</math> is the volume of <math>A.</math>

==Definition for functions==

The rearrangement of a non-negative, measurable real-valued function <math>f</math> whose level sets <math>f^{-1}(y)</math> (for <math>y \in \R_{\geq 0}</math>) have finite measure is
<math display=block>f^*(x) = \int_0^\infty \mathbb{I}_{\{y: f(y)>t\}^*}(x) \, dt,</math>
where <math>\mathbb{I}_A</math> denotes the [[indicator function]] of the set <math>A.</math>  
In words, the value of <math>f^*(x)</math> gives the height <math>t</math> for which the radius of the symmetric
rearrangement of <math>\{y: f(y) > t\}</math> is equal to <math>x.</math> We have the following motivation for this definition. Because the identity
<math display=block>g(x) = \int_0^\infty \mathbb{I}_{\{y: g(y)>t\}}(x) \, dt,</math>
holds for any non-negative function <math>g,</math> the above definition is the unique definition that forces the identity <math>\mathbb{I}_{A}^* = \mathbb{I}_{A^*}</math> to hold.

==Properties==
[[File:Function and its symmetric decreasing rearrangement.svg|500px|thumb|Function and its symmetric decreasing rearrangement preserve the measure of level sets.]]

The function <math>f^*</math> is a symmetric and decreasing function whose level sets have the same measure as the level sets of <math>f,</math> that is,
<math display=block>|\{x: f^*(x)>t\}| = |\{x: f(x)>t\}|.</math>

If <math>f</math> is a function in <math>L^p,</math> then
<math display=block>\|f\|_{L^p} = \|f^*\|_{L^p}.</math>

The [[Hardy–Littlewood inequality]] holds, that is,
<math display=block>\int fg \leq \int f^* g^*.</math>

Further, the [[Pólya–Szegő inequality]] holds.  This says that if <math>1 \leq p < \infty</math> and if <math>f \in W^{1,p}</math> then
<math display=block>\|\nabla f^*\|_p \leq \|\nabla f\|_p.</math>

The symmetric decreasing rearrangement is order preserving and decreases <math>L^p</math> distance, that is,
<math display=block>f \leq g \text{ implies }  f^* \leq g^*</math>
and
<math display=block>\|f - g\|_{L^p} \geq \|f^* - g^*\|_{L^p}.</math>

==Applications==

The Pólya&ndash;Szegő inequality yields, in the limit case, with <math>p = 1,</math> the [[isoperimetric inequality]].  Also, one can use some relations with harmonic functions to prove the [[Rayleigh–Faber–Krahn inequality]].

==Nonsymmetric decreasing rearrangement==

We can also define <math>f^*</math> as a function on the nonnegative real numbers rather than on all of <math>\R^n.</math><ref name=bennettsharpley>{{cite book|last1=Bennett|first1=Colin|last2=Sharpley|first2=Robert|title=Interpolation of Operators|year=1988|isbn=978-0-120-88730-9}}</ref>  Let <math>(E, \mu)</math> be a [[σ-finite measure|σ-finite measure space]], and let <math>f : E\to[-\infty,\infty]</math> be a [[measurable function]] that takes only finite (that is, real) values [[almost everywhere|μ-a.e.]] (where "<math>\mu</math>-a.e." means except possibly on a set of <math>\mu</math>-measure zero).  We define the '''distribution function''' <math>\mu_f : [0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]</math> by the rule
<math display=block>\mu_f(s)=\mu\{x\in E : \vert f(x)\vert >s\}.</math>
We can now define the '''decreasing rearrangment''' (or, sometimes, '''nonincreasing rearrangement''') of <math>f</math> as the function <math>f^* : [0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]</math> by the rule
<math display=block>f^*(t)=\inf\{s\in[0,\infty] : \mu_f(s)\leq t\}.</math>
Note that this version of the decreasing rearrangement is not symmetric, as it is only defined on the nonnegative real numbers. However, it inherits many of the same properties listed above as the symmetric version, namely:

* <math>f</math> and <math>f^*</math> are '''equimeasurable''', that is, they have the same distribution function.
* The Hardy-Littlewood inequality holds, that is, <math>\int_E|fg|\;d\mu\leq\int_0^\infty f^*(t)g^*(t)\;dt.</math>
* <math>\vert f\vert\leq\vert g\vert</math> <math>\mu</math>-a.e. implies <math>f^*\leq g^*.</math>
* <math>(af)^*=|a|f^*</math> for all real numbers <math>a.</math>
* <math>(f+g)^*(t_1+t_2) \leq f^*(t_1)+g^*(t_2)</math> for all <math>t_1,t_2\in[0,\infty).</math>
* <math>|f_n|\uparrow|f|</math> <math>\mu</math>-a.e. implies <math>f_n^*\uparrow f^*.</math>
* <math>\left(\vert f\vert^p\right)^*=(f^*)^p</math> for all positive real numbers <math>p.</math>
* <math>\|f\|_{L_p(E)}=\|f^*\|_{L_p[0,\infty)}</math> for all positive real numbers <math>p.</math>
* <math>\|f\|_{L_\infty(E)}=f^*(0).</math>

The (nonsymmetric) decreasing rearrangement function arises often in the theory of rearrangement-invariant Banach function spaces. Especially important is the following:
:'''Luxemburg Representation Theorem.'''  Let <math>\rho</math> be a rearrangement-invariant Banach function norm over a resonant measure space <math>(E, \mu).</math> Then there exists a (possibly not unique) rearrangement-invariant function norm <math>\overline{\rho}</math> on <math>[0,\infty)</math> such that <math>\rho(f)=\overline{\rho}(f^*)</math> for all nonnegative measurable functions <math>f : E \to [0,\infty]</math> which are finite-valued <math>\mu</math>-a.e.
Note that the definitions of all the terminology in the above theorem (that is, Banach function norms, rearrangement-invariant Banach function spaces, and resonant measure spaces) can be found in sections 1 and 2 of Bennett and Sharpley's book (cf. the references below).
